h: Repentance That Turns Sorrow into Joy

p: בְּמִזְמוֹר שֶׁל שַׁבָּת כְּתִיב טוֹב לְהוֹדוֹת לַהַשֵּׁם וּלְזַמֵּר לְשִׁמְךָ עֶלְיוֹן.
— In the psalm for Shabbat it is written, “It is good to give thanks to Hashem and sing to Your name, Most High.”
טוֹב לְהוֹדוֹת — הַיְינוּ בְּחִינַת תְּשׁוּבָה,
— “It is good to acknowledge” refers to repentance,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק יט): שֶׁכָּל מִי שֶׁמּוֹדֶה עַל פְּשָׁעָיו נִיצּוֹל מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנֹּם,
— for Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer, chapter 19, teaches that whoever acknowledges his transgressions is saved from the judgment of Gehinnom,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר מוֹדֶה וְעוֹזֵב יְרוּחָם.
— as it says, “One who confesses and abandons them will find mercy.”
וְכֵן אִיתָא (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה כב): כָּךְ הִיא כֹּחָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵי, עָמַד אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן וְאָמַר מִזְמוֹר שִׁיר לְיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת.
— Likewise at the end of Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 22: such is the power of repentance, and so forth. Adam arose and recited “A psalm, a song for the day of Shabbat.”
וְהַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב וּלְזַמֵּר, שֶׁהוּא בְּחִינַת שִׂמְחָה וּרְנָנָה,
— “To sing” signifies joy and exultation,
הֲגַם דְּאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג ח א), דְּמַאן דְּתָב לְקַמֵּי דְמָארֵיהּ, בְּמַאן אַנְפִּין יְקוּם קַמֵּיהּ?
— although the holy Zohar, Part III 8a, asks: one who repents before his Master—with what countenance can he stand before Him?
הָא וַדַּאי בְּרוּחַ תְּבִירָא, בְּרוּחַ עֲצִיב. אָן הוּא שִׂמְחָה? אָן הוּא רְנָנָה וְכוּלֵי?
— Surely with a broken spirit, a sorrowful spirit. Where is joy? Where is exultation, and so forth?
רַק עַל יְדֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים וְהַלְוִיִּם בַּעֲבוֹדַת קָרְבָּנוֹ אַשְׁלִימוּ שִׂמְחָה וּרְנָנָה בְּגִינֵיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
— Only the priests and Levites, through the service of his offering, complete joy and exultation on his behalf; see there.
אָמְנָם קְדוּשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת פּוֹעֵל לְהִתְעוֹרְרֻת הַתְּשׁוּבָה, וְעִם כָּל זֶה לְזַמֵּר וּלְרַנֵּן בְּשִׂמְחָה,
— Shabbat’s holiness, however, awakens repentance while allowing one to sing and exult joyfully,
שֶׁקְּדוּשַּׁת שַׁבָּת פּוֹעֵל לִהְיוֹת בְּחִינַת תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה,
— for Shabbat’s holiness brings repentance from love,
אֲשֶׁר עַל יְדֵי זֶה נִצְמָח עוֹד הַשִּׂמְחָה בַּלֵּב,
— through which joy additionally grows within the heart,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּיוֹם הָנִיחַ הַשֵּׁם לְךָ מֵעָצְבְּךָ וּמֵרָגְזֶךָ וְגוֹמֵר,
— as it says, “On the day Hashem gives you rest from your sorrow and turmoil,” and so forth,
שֶׁנִּדְרַשׁ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק א מח רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב וּשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת) עַל יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת, שֶׁהוּא יוֹם הָנִיחַ הַמְיוּחָד לְנַיְיחָא.
— expounded in the holy Zohar, Part I, beginning of 48b and elsewhere, concerning Shabbat, the day of rest particularly designated for repose.
וְדִקְדְּקוּ מִדְּלָא כְתִיב בְּהָנִיחַ וְגוֹמֵר וּכְתִיב בְּיוֹם הָנִיחַ, מַשְׁמַע דְּעַל יוֹם הַמְיוּחָד לִמְנוּחָה קָאֵי.
— They inferred that because it says “on the day of giving rest,” rather than simply “when giving rest,” it refers to the day specifically devoted to rest.
וְזֶהוּ הָעִנְיָן הַנִּזְכָּר בְּפָרָשָׁה זוֹ, שֶׁאָמַר יוֹסֵף לְהַשְּׁבָטִים: וְעַתָּה אַל תֵּעָצְבוּ וְאַל יִחַר בְּעֵינֵיכֶם וְגוֹמֵר,
— This explains Joseph’s words to the tribes in this portion: “Now, do not be sorrowful or distressed,” and so forth,
כִּי לְמִחְיָה שְׁלָחַנִי אֱלֹהִים לִפְנֵיכֶם.
— “for God sent me ahead of you to preserve life.”
וְלִכְאוֹרָה מְחוּסַּר הֲבָנָה, מַה נִּיחֵם אוֹתָם בָּזֶה כִּי לְמִחְיָה שְׁלָחַנִי? וְכִי בָּזֶה יִהְיֶה תְּרוּפָה לְמַכְאוֹבָם?
— How does “He sent me to preserve life” console them? Can that heal their pain?
הָא הֵם לֹא נִתְכַּוְּנוּ לְטוֹבָה,
— Their intention was not benevolent,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (נָזִיר כג.): מִי שֶׁנִּתְכַּוֵּון לַעֲלוֹת בְּיָדוֹ וְכוּלֵי, וְעָלָה בְּיָדוֹ בְּשַׂר טָלֶה, טָעוּן כַּפָּרָה וּסְלִיחָה.
— and Nazir 23a teaches: one who intended to obtain, and so forth, but obtained lamb’s meat, still requires atonement and forgiveness.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 8:1: “After Adam heard from Cain, who told him, ‘I repented and was reconciled’ … he said of this, ‘Such is the power of repentance’: it is effective even through verbal confession alone, though one has not yet abandoned the sin as one should, until He who knows hidden things testifies about him. … At once he stood and said, ‘A psalm, a song for the day of Shabbat,’ for there it is written, ‘It is good to acknowledge Hashem,’ and it does not say ‘and abandon,’ as in ‘One who confesses and abandons them will find mercy.’ This is the power of Shabbat: words alone are effective as well. … On Shabbat it becomes clear that Israel are bound at their root to the Blessed One, and that ‘our will is to do Your will’; therefore verbal confession is then effective, and this is what we say, ‘It is good to acknowledge Hashem.’ … At the entrance of Shabbat it is written, ‘God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good,’ … and this is revealed on Shabbat, when everything becomes very good, good that emerges from within evil. Therefore Shabbat is a time of repentance.”

p: אוּלָם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר בָּזֶה עַל פִּי מַה דְּאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת לד:), דִּפְלִיגִי: דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים לֹא נִתְנַבְּאוּ אֶלָּא לְבַעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה,
— We can explain this through the dispute in Berakhot 34b: Rabbi Yochanan says that all the prophets prophesied only concerning penitents,
אֲבָל צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים — עַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה וְגוֹמֵר.
— whereas concerning the completely righteous, “No eye has seen,” and so forth.
וְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר: מָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין, צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים אֵינָם עוֹמְדִין.
— Rabbi Abbahu says: where penitents stand, the completely righteous do not stand.
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, וְלֹא פְלִיגִי, רַק תָּלוּי בְּאֵיכוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה,
— Both may be the words of the living God, without disagreement, depending instead upon the quality of repentance.
דְּאִיתָא (יוֹמָא פו:) דְּעַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה, וְהַיְינוּ מִיִּרְאַת הָעוֹנֶשׁ, זְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוֹת לוֹ כִּשְׁגָגוֹת,
— Yoma 86b teaches that through repentance from fear, meaning fear of punishment, deliberate sins become inadvertent sins,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה, זְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוֹת לוֹ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת.
— whereas through repentance from love, deliberate sins become merits.
וְהִנֵּה צָרִיךְ לְהָבִין מַה עִנְיַן שֶׁהַזְּדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוֹת כִּשְׁגָגוֹת,
— We must understand what it means for deliberate sins to become inadvertent ones.
מִמָּה נַפְשָׁךְ, אִם נִמְחַל הֶעָוֹן לְגַמְרֵי, לֹא יוּשְׁאַר מִמֶּנּוּ שׁוּם רוֹשֶׁם,
— Either way: if the sin has been completely forgiven, no trace should remain,

p: רַק הָעִנְיָן הוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (קִידּוּשִׁין נט), דְּאֵין מַחֲשָׁבָה מוֹצִיא מִידֵי מַעֲשֶׂה,
— The explanation follows Kiddushin 59: thought cannot undo an act,
אֲבָל מַחֲשָׁבָה מוֹצִיא מִידֵי מַחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ כְּמַעֲשֶׂה,
— but thought can undo a thought that has not become an act.
וְכֵן דִּבּוּר, אָתֵי דִיבּוּר וּמְבַטֵּל דִּיבּוּר.
— Likewise with speech: a later utterance can cancel an earlier utterance.
וְהִנֵּה כַּאֲשֶׁר עָבַר אָדָם עֲבֵירָה בְּמֵזִיד, הָיָה הַפְּגָם בְּמַעֲשֶׂה וּבְמַחֲשָׁבָה,
— When a person deliberately transgressed, the blemish affected both action and thought,
שֶׁעָשָׂה בְּכַוָּנָה בִּשְׁאָט בְּנֶפֶשׁ.
— since he acted intentionally and defiantly.
וְכַאֲשֶׁר מֵשִׂים אֶל לִבּוֹ יִרְאַת הָעוֹנֶשׁ מַה שֶּׁיַּגִּיעַ אֵלָיו, הוּא מִתְנַחֵם וּמִתְחָרֵט עַל הֶעָבָר בְּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ,
— When he takes to heart fear of the punishment awaiting him, he changes his mind and inwardly regrets the past,
וְכֵן בְּדִיבּוּר, שֶׁשָּׁב וּמִתְוַדֶּה,
— and likewise through speech, by repenting and confessing.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה עוֹקֵר הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה רִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁל הָעֲבֵירָה.
— Through this he uproots the original sinful intention.
אֲבָל מַעֲשֵׂה הָעֲבֵירָה נִשְׁאָר בְּתָקְפּוֹ, כְּמוֹ הַשּׁוֹגֵג שֶׁעָשָׂה מַעֲשֵׂה הָעֲבֵירָה בְּלֹא כַוָּנָה,
— The sinful act, however, remains intact, like that of one who committed the transgression unintentionally.
וְנַעֲשׂוֹת לוֹ כִּשְׁגָגוֹת.
— Thus his sins become inadvertent transgressions.
וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים נִשְׁאָר לוֹ פְּגָם שֶׁל הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, שֶׁנִּצְרָךְ לוֹ כַּפָּרָה וְסִיגּוּפִים,
— The blemish of the act still remains and requires atonement and self-discipline.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַשָּׁב מֵאַהֲבָה, שֶׁמֵּאִיר לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּמְתַקֵּן גּוּף הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוֹת לוֹ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת,
— But when one repents from love, Hashem illuminates him and repairs the very act, so that his sins become merits.
וְלָכֵן הוּא יוֹתֵר מְעוּלֶּה מִצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ זְכֻיּוֹת חֲדָשִׁים,
— He is therefore higher than the completely righteous person, for he has new merits,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין בְּכֹחַ הַצַּדִּיק מֵעִקָּרוֹ לְהַגִּיעַ לִזְכֻיּוֹת כָּאֵלּוּ,
— which one righteous from the outset cannot attain,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב קפד א): דְּלֵית נְהוֹרָא אֶלָּא הַהוּא דְּנָפִיק מִגּוֹ חֲשׁוֹכָא, וְלֵית טָבָא אֶלָּא מִגּוֹ בִּישָׁא,
— as in Zohar, Part II 184a: there is no light except that which emerges from darkness, and no good except that which emerges from evil.
וְאָז הוּא נַעֲשֶׂה טוֹב מְאֹד.
— It then becomes “very good.”
וְהִנֵּה הַשָּׁב מִיִּרְאַת הָעוֹנֶשׁ הוּא תָּמִיד בְּעִצָּבוֹן עַל הֶעָבָר, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמַּרְגִּישׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁנִּשְׁאָר עָלָיו רוֹשֶׁם הַפְּגָם שֶׁל הַמַּעֲשֶׂה,
— One who repents from fear of punishment remains sorrowful over the past, sensing that the trace of the act’s blemish remains upon him.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא חָרֵד בְּנַפְשׁוֹ גַּם עַל הֶעָתִיד, שֶׁלֹּא יְסִיתֵהוּ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע עוֹד,
— He consequently also fears for the future, lest the evil inclination entice him again,
כְּעִנְיַן הַיָּדוּעַ שֶׁעֲבֵירָה גּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵירָה, מִצַּד הַפְּגָם שֶׁנִּשְׁאַר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ מֵהֶעָבָר.
— in accordance with the familiar principle that one transgression leads to another, because of the past blemish remaining in his soul.

p: וְהִנֵּה כַּאֲשֶׁר רָאָה יוֹסֵף שֶׁנִּתְחָרְטוּ אֶחָיו עַל מְכִירָתוֹ,
— When Joseph saw that his brothers regretted selling him,
כְּאָמְרָם אֲבָל אֲשֵׁמִים אֲנַחְנוּ עַל אָחִינוּ וְגוֹמֵר, עַל כֵּן בָּאָה אֵלֵינוּ הַצָּרָה הַזֹּאת,
— as they said, “Indeed, we are guilty concerning our brother,” and so forth, “therefore this trouble has come upon us,”
וְזֶה הָיָה מִיִּרְאַת הָעוֹנֶשׁ, כַּאֲשֶׁר הִרְגִּישׁוּ שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִצַּד הָעוֹנֶשׁ שֶׁל הַמְּכִירָה,
— this arose from fear of punishment, as they recognized it as punishment for the sale.
וְיָדַע שֶׁעַל כָּל פָּנִים יִהְיֶה נִשְׁאָר בְּנַפְשָׁם הָעֶצֶב עַל הֶעָבָר, וְגַם הָרוֹגֶז וְהַחֲרָדָה עַל הֶעָתִיד, כַּנִּזְכָּר.
— He knew that sorrow over the past would therefore remain within them, as would turmoil and fear for the future, as explained.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר לָהֶם וְעַתָּה אַל תֵּעָצְבוּ, וְאֵין וְעַתָּה אֶלָּא תְּשׁוּבָה,
— He therefore told them, “Now, do not be sorrowful”; “now” signifies repentance,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כא וּשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת).
— as stated in Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 21, and elsewhere.
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁעֲשִׂיתֶם לֹא יִשָּׁאֵר בְּנַפְשְׁכֶם שׁוּם עֶצֶב, גַּם אִם הוּא מִיִּרְאַת הָעוֹנֶשׁ,
— Your repentance will leave no sorrow within you, even if it arose from fear of punishment,
מִפְּנֵי שֶׁגַּם מֵהַמַּעֲשֶׂה לֹא יִשָּׁאֵר שׁוּם פְּגָם, כִּי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה הָיָה לְטוֹבָה,
— because no blemish will remain even from the act, for the act proved beneficial:
כִּי לְמִחְיָה שְׁלָחַנִי אֱלֹהִים לִפְנֵיכֶם.
— “God sent me ahead of you to preserve life.”
כִּי גַּם יוֹסֵף בְּעַצְמוֹ הוּא מְפוּיָּיס בָּזֶה, כִּי עַל יְדֵי זֶה נַעֲשָׂה מוֹשֵׁל בְּכָל אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם.
— Joseph himself was reconciled to it, since it made him ruler over all Egypt.
וְעַל הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁלָּכֶם אָתֵי מַחֲשֶׁבֶת הַחֲרָטָה וְדִיבּוּר שֶׁל הַוִּידּוּי וּמוֹצִיא מִיַּד מַחֲשָׁבָה הָרָעָה, כָּאָמוּר.
— As for your intention, the thought of regret and the spoken confession cancel the evil intention, as explained.

paragraphs.text: Connection: Or HaChaim likewise distinguishes the brothers’ harmful intention from the beneficial outcome of their deed, illuminating why Joseph can describe the act as a means of preserving life. Rav Tzadok makes the treatment of their intention explicit: regret and spoken confession cancel the evil thought. His explanation therefore combines the providential good achieved through the act with the brothers’ repentance for what they intended.

p: וְעַל זֶה מוֹרֶה קְדוּשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת, שֶׁבְּשַׁבָּת חוֹשֵׁב כָּל אֶחָד הָעוֹבֵר עָלָיו כָּל יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה,
— Shabbat’s holiness points to this: on Shabbat each person considers what has occurred to him throughout the working days,
וְהוּא מוֹדֶה וּמִתְחָרֵט, אַךְ זֶה גּוֹרֵם לוֹ עֲצִיבוּ דְרוּחָא.
— and acknowledges and regrets it, but this causes him sadness of spirit.
וְיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת מֵנִיחַ לוֹ מֵהָעִצָּבוֹן,
— Shabbat grants him rest from sorrow,
דְּשַׁבָּת הוּא מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא,
— for Shabbat resembles the World to Come.
שֶׁאָז יְבָרֵר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים הַלָּלוּ,
— Then Hashem will clarify: “Even if your sins are like these years,
שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית וְעַד עַכְשָׁיו, כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ, (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שַׁבָּת פט:),
— ordered and unfolding from the six days of Creation until now, they will become white as snow,” as stated in Shabbat 89b,
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוֹת לוֹ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת.
— meaning that they become merits.
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁמֵּאִיר לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁכָּךְ עָלָה בַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה לְפָנָיו,
— Hashem illuminates for him that this arose in His thought:
לִהְיוֹת נְהוֹרָא דְּנָפַק מִגּוֹ חֲשׁוֹכָא, שֶׁיְּתַקֵּן עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה טוֹב מְאֹד.
— that light should emerge from darkness, repaired through repentance from love to become “very good.”
וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּיוֹם הָנִיחַ הַשֵּׁם לְךָ מֵעָצְבְּךָ — עַל הֶעָבָר,
— Thus, “On the day Hashem gives you rest from your sorrow”—concerning the past,
וּמֵרָגְזֶךָ — שֶׁהוּא עַל הֶעָתִיד, שֶׁמְּפַחֵד שֶׁלֹּא יְסִיתֵהוּ עוֹד,
— “and your turmoil”—concerning the future, fearing that the evil inclination may again entice him,
שֶׁכֵּן דַּרְכּוֹ שֶׁל יֵצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁהוֹלֵךְ מֵהַקַּלּוֹת אֶל הַחֲמוּרוֹת, (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שַׁבָּת קה:).
— for the evil inclination progresses from lesser matters to graver ones, as stated in Shabbat 105b.
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ פְּגַם שְׁגָגוֹת, עֲבֵירָה גּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵירָה.
— Since the blemish of inadvertent sins remains, one transgression leads to another.
אָמְנָם עַל יְדֵי הַשַּׁבָּת, שֶׁזּוֹכֶה שֶׁיִּהְיוּ נַעֲשׂוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, אָז אֵין לוֹ פַחַד מֵרוֹגֶז הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע.
— Through Shabbat, however, he merits their becoming merits and no longer fears the evil inclination’s turmoil.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר לָהֶם יוֹסֵף אַחַר כָּךְ אַל תִּרְגְּזוּ בַּדָּרֶךְ,
— This is Joseph’s later statement, “Do not be agitated on the way,”
הַיְינוּ שֶׁגַּם עַל לְהַבָּא לֹא יַעֲלֶה בְּנַפְשָׁם שׁוּם פַּחַד וְרוֹגֶז, שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְקַן וְלֹא נִשְׁאַר שׁוּם פְּגָם מֵהֶעָוֹן הַזֶּה.
— meaning that no fear or turmoil should arise within them concerning the future either, for this sin was already repaired and no blemish remained.
וְזֶה הָיָה גַּם כֵּן מִמַּה שֶּׁהִטְעִים לָהֶם מִבְּחִינַת קְדוּשַּׁת שַׁבָּת בִּסְעוּדָתוֹ,
— This too resulted from the taste of Shabbat’s holiness he imparted through his meal,
שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה וְאֵין וְהָכֵן אֶלָּא שַׁבָּת.
— for Bereishit Rabbah teaches that “prepare” refers to Shabbat.
וְאַף שֶׁקִּיבֵּל מֵהֶם עוֹד בִּנְיָמִין,
— Although he still took Benjamin from them,
בְּוַדַּאי יָדַע שֶׁיִּתְוַדַּע לָהֶם, שֶׁהֲרֵי רָצָה לְהוֹדִיעַ לְאָבִיו וּלְשַׂמְּחוֹ וּלְהַחֲיוֹת רוּחוֹ,
— he certainly knew that he would reveal himself to them, since he wished to inform his father, gladden him, and revive his spirit.
אַךְ רָצָה עוֹד לְבָרֵר אוֹתָם, שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן עֲדַיִין הַכֹּל,
— He wished, however, to refine them further, since not everything had yet been repaired.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה צג): כָּל הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁדִּיבֵּר יְהוּדָה לְיוֹסֵף הָיָה בָּהֶם פִּיּוּס לְיוֹסֵף וּפִיּוּס לְאֶחָיו וְכוּלֵי.
— Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 93, states: everything Judah said to Joseph contained appeasement for Joseph and appeasement for his brothers, and so forth.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ וְלֹא יָכוֹל יוֹסֵף לְהִתְאַפֵּק, שֶׁכְּבָר תִּקְּנוּ הַכֹּל,
— Then “Joseph could no longer restrain himself,” for they had already repaired everything.
וְאָמַר לָהֶם וְעַתָּה אַל תֵּעָצְבוּ עַל הֶעָבָר, וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמַר לָהֶם אַל תִּרְגְּזוּ בַּדָּרֶךְ עַל הֶעָתִיד.
— He told them “Now, do not be sorrowful” concerning the past, and afterward “Do not be agitated on the way” concerning the future.
כִּי עַל יְדֵי קְדוּשַּׁת שַׁבָּת נִמְצָא הַכֹּחַ הַזֶּה לִהְיוֹת נַעֲשׂוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת,
— Shabbat’s holiness supplies this power for sins to become merits,
וְנִכְנָס נַיְיחָא בַּלֵּב, מֵעָצְבְּךָ עַל הֶעָבָר וּמֵרָגְזֶךָ עַל הֶעָתִיד.
— and repose enters the heart, relieving sorrow over the past and turmoil concerning the future.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּמְּכִילְתָּא (בְּשַׁלַּח וַיִּסַּע פָּרָשָׁה ה), עַל פָּסוּק שׁוֹמֵר שַׁבָּת וְגוֹמֵר וְשׁוֹמֵר יָדוֹ מֵעֲשׂוֹת כָּל רָע,
— As the Mekhilta, Beshalach, Vayissa chapter 5, teaches on “One who keeps Shabbat,” and so forth, “and guards his hand from doing any evil”:
שֶׁכָּל מִי שֶׁמְּשַׁמֵּר אֶת הַשַּׁבָּת מְרוּחָק מִן הָעֲבֵירָה.
— whoever observes Shabbat is distanced from transgression.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר לָהֶם אַל תִּרְגְּזוּ בַּדָּרֶךְ.
— This is why he told them, “Do not be agitated on the way.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Tzidkat HaTzadik §40: “The essence of repentance is to reach the point at which God illuminates a person’s eyes so that deliberate sins become merits: he recognizes and understands that all he sinned was also within God’s will. This is as the Sages said concerning the three verses: ‘You turned their hearts backward,’ ‘whom I have harmed,’ and so forth. It is like the Divine knowledge and human choice explained by the Arizal at the end of Sefer Arba Me’ot Shekel Kesef: both are true, each in its own domain. In the domain of choice there is no place for foreknowledge; in the domain of foreknowledge there is truly no place for choice. When one attains this immense light, all one’s deliberate sins return within the depths of God’s knowledge. He, His knowledge, and His will are all one; since God willed it so, everything becomes merit, and one attains the complete atonement of Yom Kippur.”

paragraphs.text: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Vayassa 6:1: “Perhaps you will say: What reward does one who observes Shabbat receive? Scripture teaches: “Happy is the person who does this, and the one who holds fast to it: who keeps Shabbat from profaning it and keeps his hand from doing any evil.” Thus we learn that whoever observes Shabbat even under difficult circumstances is saved from transgression.”
